question_text:
Historians of the Haldrenne coppersmiths' guild have long explained its lead seals, crimped onto the handle of every finished kettle, as a guarantee of quality, a sign that only sound metal left the town. Yet the smiths of nearby Ostrevik, who worked the same ore to the same pattern and sold to the same buyers, used no seals at all, and their kettles drew no more complaints. In Haldrenne, each master received a fixed number of seals every season, and a kettle without one could not be offered in the guild's market hall; a master who ran short bought spare seals from a colleague at a set price. Every seal bore the guild's emblem alone, and no record was kept of which kettles proved flawed. Complaints about defects, by contrast, were settled by wardens who examined the kettle itself. These details suggest that the seals chiefly served

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: to reassure distant buyers about the metal's soundness, since they could not test a kettle before purchasing it.
answer_b: to bring revenue into the guild, since masters who ran short of seals had to pay for extra ones.
answer_c: to trace a defective kettle to its maker, since a sealed kettle could be brought back to the workshop responsible.
answer_d: to limit the total number of kettles the masters could sell, since the guild controlled the supply of seals that sales required.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer. The passage says each master received a fixed number of seals per season and that a kettle without a seal could not be offered in the market hall. Together these show that the guild's fixed supply of seals set a ceiling on how many kettles its masters could sell. A master who ran short could buy seals from a colleague, but that only moved seals among masters; the guild alone issued them, so the total, and with it the number of kettles that could be sold, stayed fixed. The other details point the same way: Ostrevik's unsealed kettles drew no more complaints, so the seals were not needed for quality, and complaints were settled by inspecting the kettle itself rather than by consulting seals.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It rescues the received quality-guarantee account by assuming buyers could not judge kettles for themselves. The passage undercuts this: Ostrevik's smiths sold to the same buyers without seals and drew no more complaints, and defects were judged by examining the kettle, not by relying on the seal.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It fits the salient detail that masters who ran short had to pay for extra seals, but the passage says they bought them from a colleague at a set price, not from the guild, and nothing in the passage shows the guild receiving any money for seals.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. Tracing a faulty kettle to its maker would require a seal that identified the workshop, but every seal bore the guild's emblem alone, so a seal could not point to any particular maker. The passage therefore rules this purpose out.

question_text:
Scholars of the Tarnmoor ore district have long explained the numbered brass token that each miner hung on a pithead board before descending as a safeguard, a way of showing rescuers who was underground. Yet the number on each token was also chalked on every tub its owner filled, and the board was cleared only once the day's tubs had been weighed. In the neighboring Lowgill workings, equally deep and equally gassy, miners carried no tokens, and a foreman's list of names served for any head count. The Tarnmoor company paid a smith each winter to restamp worn tokens, an expense its books entered under the weighing house. Theft of ore, by contrast, was policed at the weighing house, where a clerk inspected every tub for stones and short loads, just as clerks did at Lowgill. These details suggest that the token system chiefly served

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: to speed rescue after a fall of rock, since rescuers would read the board to learn which men were trapped.
answer_b: to link each load of ore to the miner who raised it, since the token numbers tied output to the weighing records.
answer_c: to deter pilfering from the workings, since every tub was marked with the number of the miner who filled it.
answer_d: to assign each miner to a working face for the shift, since his numbered token marked his place on the pithead board.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it is the purpose the details support together. The token's number was chalked on every tub its owner filled, the board was cleared only after the day's tubs were weighed, and the company's books entered the cost of restamping tokens under the weighing house. Meanwhile, the equally deep and gassy Lowgill workings managed head counts with a foreman's list and no tokens, and theft was handled by a clerk's inspection of every tub, as at Lowgill, where there were no tokens at all. That leaves tying each miner's output to the weighing as the tokens' chief function.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It restates the received safety account, but the passage shows that the equally deep and gassy Lowgill workings managed head counts with a foreman's list and no tokens, so safety cannot explain what the tokens were chiefly for. The chalked numbers, the board's clearing only after weighing, and the restamping cost booked under the weighing house all point instead to the weighing.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It reads the chalked numbers as an anti-theft device, but the passage places theft control in the clerk's inspection of every tub for stones and short loads, an inspection also made at Lowgill, where miners carried no tokens. Policing theft therefore did not depend on the tokens.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It treats the pithead board as a work roster, but nothing in the passage connects the tokens to where a miner worked. It also leaves unexplained why the board was cleared only after weighing, why each token's number was chalked on its owner's tubs, and why the token expense was entered under the weighing house.

question_text:
Historians have long held that the tinted glass bottles required of apothecaries in the city of Marrowick, amber for one class of drug and green for another, were meant to prevent dosing errors, since a clerk could supposedly judge a preparation's strength at a glance. Yet the guild's own scheme gave strong and dilute preparations of the same drug an identical tint. Guild minutes record that inspectors checked each spring only whether tinted glass stood on shop shelves, never what a bottle held or at what strength. And in Dunhallow, a port of similar size that stocked the same drugs but whose council barred unlicensed healers from the market, apothecaries kept their medicines in plain glass, whereas Marrowick's market admitted unlicensed healers alongside the guild's shops. Doses, meanwhile, were stated in numerals on the wrapper of every prescription. These details suggest that the tint requirement served chiefly

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: to let patients tell strong preparations from dilute ones, since they could learn the guild's color scheme with use.
answer_b: to help assistants keep drug classes sorted on shelves, since each tint corresponded to a class of remedy.
answer_c: to let inspectors confirm that bottles held what was claimed, since they examined shop shelves every spring.
answer_d: to mark remedies as guild-sold, since the tint signaled a guild shop's stock and said nothing about how much to take.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer. The passage undercuts the received view that tints prevented dosing errors: strong and dilute versions of a drug shared a tint, inspectors never checked contents or strength, and doses were written in numerals on every prescription anyway. It also shows that the tint did not sort stock for its own sake, because Dunhallow, stocking the same drugs, used plain glass. The difference the passage notes is that Dunhallow barred unlicensed healers from its market, whereas Marrowick's market admitted them beside the guild's shops. Taken together, the details suggest that the required tint served as a visible sign that a remedy came from a guild shop, setting guild stock apart from that of the unlicensed healers who sold in the same market.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It rescues the received account by assuming patients could learn to read strength from color, but the passage says strong and dilute preparations of the same drug had an identical tint, so the tint could not convey strength.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It fits the detail that tints corresponded to classes of drug, but Dunhallow stocked the same drugs and used plain glass, so sorting remedies into classes did not require tinted bottles. The one difference the passage notes between the two cities is the presence of unlicensed healers in Marrowick's market, not any difference in how stock was sorted, so sorting does not explain why Marrowick required tint.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. The passage says inspectors checked only whether tinted glass was present, never what a bottle held, so the tint cannot have been meant to let them confirm contents.
